meta.blurb: Ines Marlow loves her desk by the window at the Harbourgate Tram Company, until Jonah Pike takes the desk opposite. One job, eight weeks and one stubborn rival. Can two people who must win ever learn to share the road?
meta.bible: Ines Marlow: a sharp, hard-working tram planner at desk three, proud, tidy, afraid of being ordinary; grew up above a laundry and counted buses from the window; her mother cleaned offices. Jonah Pike: the new planner at desk four, calm, tall, always humming, drinks tea from a chipped blue mug; his grandfather drove trams. Alfie Pike: Jonah's grandfather, 78, retired tram driver of Line 9, gentle and funny. Mrs Faro: the director of planning, fair and watchful. Priya: Ines's friend at desk one, kind and honest. Tomas: the office gossip at desk five. Mr Garrity: a consultant from Garrity and Lowe who offers the Board a cheap plan. Harbourgate: the harbour city. Harbourgate Tram Company: the workplace, second floor, a big window over the harbour. The Clock: the old timetable software. Line 9: the old tram line, closing for good. Line 12: the new line; the prize is the post of Head of Planning for it. Gull Street: a busy crossing. Quay Hill: a steep street. The Board: the group of city leaders who choose; they meet at the Harbour Hall. The task: eight weeks, two plans, one job. Ines's plan is fast trams; Jonah's plan is frequent stops that wait for people. The plan they build together is called fast spine, gentle branches. Ending: Mrs Faro makes two Heads of Planning, Ines and Jonah; they share one desk island, her yellow mug beside his blue one. Voice and tone: warm, quick, funny, gently romantic, a slow-burning rivalry; no bad language, no bad behaviour.

B1B2: Every morning, Ines Marlow arrived before anyone else and watched the harbour wake up from her desk. She had worked at the Harbourgate Tram Company for six years, and she knew every timetable by heart.
On Monday, the director, Mrs Faro, walked in with a tall stranger and pointed at the empty desk across from Ines. His name was Jonah Pike, and he was a new planner.
Jonah hummed softly while he worked, and he drank tea from a blue mug with a chip in it. Ines found it very hard to think, and she did not know why it bothered her so much.

Mrs Faro called everyone together and told them that the city was building a new tram line, Line 12. She would give the job of Head of Planning to the author of the best plan, and the Board would decide in eight weeks.

At lunch, Ines told her friend Priya that the new job would be hers, whatever it took. Priya laughed kindly and said that Ines already worked far too hard and that she should save some energy for living.

The printer had been broken for weeks, and Ines had complained about it to everyone. Jonah fixed it in a minute with a small screwdriver, and the whole office clapped, which made Ines feel even more annoyed.
Ines stayed at her desk long after dark, drawing maps and checking numbers. Jonah always left at five o'clock and went for a walk by the harbour, and she watched him go with a frown.
Early on Thursday, Ines went to Gull Street to measure how long people took to cross it. Jonah was already standing there with his own clipboard, and the two of them walked into each other.

Ines said that the city needed fast trams with fewer stops, because people wanted to arrive quickly. Jonah answered that old people and parents with children needed trams that stopped often and waited for them.
Mrs Faro asked each of them to explain their idea in ten minutes. She praised both plans warmly, but she said nothing at all about which one she liked best.
One evening, when everyone had gone, Ines opened the shared folder and read Jonah's plan. She felt uneasy, because it was careful and clever, and it was much better than she had expected.
The next morning there was a note on her desk, stuck to a map, with a small circle around one street. Jonah had found a mistake in her measurements, and, to her great annoyance, he was right.
Ines got her revenge by lowering Jonah's chair as far as it would go. The next day her little green plant had been moved into the sunshine, and it looked happier than it had in months.
On a rainy Tuesday, a tram broke down at Gull Street and the whole line stopped. Mrs Faro sent Ines and Jonah to sort out a new schedule, and they had to ride the next tram together.

While the rain hit the windows, Jonah said quietly that his grandfather had driven trams on Line 9 for forty years. He showed her a photo of a smiling man in a blue uniform, standing proudly beside his tram.
Ines surprised herself by telling him that she had grown up in a small flat above a laundry. As a child she had counted the buses from the window and had always wanted to make them arrive on time.
One Tuesday afternoon, the old timetable program, which everyone called the Clock, crashed without warning. Both Ines and Jonah lost a whole day of work, and they stared at the dark screens in shock.

There was no time to waste, so they spread large sheets of paper on the floor and began again by hand. Around midnight, Jonah took a sandwich from his bag, broke it in half and gave one piece to Ines.
While they worked, they both noticed that Quay Hill was too steep for a heavy tram to climb quickly. They pointed at the same spot on the map at the same moment, and they laughed.
Mrs Faro looked in and saw the two planners laughing together over the map. She smiled, but she reminded them gently that, in the end, only one of them could get the job.
That night Ines sat at home and asked herself why she wanted to win so badly. She remembered her mother, who had cleaned offices at night, and she had promised herself a desk of her own.
Line 9 was going to close for good on Friday, and Jonah asked Ines to ride it with him at sunrise. She said no, because she had too much work, but she did not sleep well that night.
In the end, Ines got up at five and walked to the Line 9 stop in the cold. Jonah was already standing there in a scarf, and he smiled as if he had been sure she would come.
On the tram, they found an old man in a blue cap, and Jonah said that he was his grandfather, Alfie. Alfie had come to say goodbye to the line he had driven for forty years.
Alfie told them funny stories about forty years on the same tracks. Then he said that a good tram should always wait a moment for the person who is running toward it.
Ines walked across to his desk and asked if she could use his idea of a waiting minute. Jonah looked surprised and then said she could take it, because a good idea belongs to everyone.
They shook hands and agreed that from now on they would compete fairly, without any tricks or secrets. The handshake lasted a little longer than a handshake should, and both of them noticed.
The presentation to the Board was only two weeks away, and the office was busy every night. Ines and Jonah worked late at their desks and ate noodles from paper boxes while they argued about numbers.
A great storm came in from the sea, and the wind shook the windows of the office. Suddenly all the lights went out, and Ines and Jonah were alone in the dark.
Because it was dark, they felt brave enough to be honest. Jonah said he was afraid of losing and having nothing to show for leaving his town, and Ines said she was afraid of being ordinary.
They sat very close, and for a moment neither of them moved. Then the lights flickered on, and they both stepped back and pretended that nothing had happened.
The following day, Ines and Jonah hardly spoke, and each of them kept their eyes on their own work. Priya noticed everything and quietly put a cup of tea on Ines's desk without a word.

Mrs Faro called the two planners into her office and spoke seriously. A cheaper company, led by Mr Garrity, had offered the Board a plan, and the Board would choose it unless the planners impressed them.
The Board wanted proof, so Mrs Faro arranged a test day on Saturday. Ines's plan would run on one stretch of the new line and Jonah's plan on another, while the Board members watched.
The morning was sunny and the fast trams ran exactly on time. But a woman with a pram reached the stop one second too late, and the tram pulled away without her.
In the afternoon, Jonah's trams waited patiently at every stop, and nobody was left behind. But the trams became crowded, and one driver complained loudly that the whole line was running late.
That evening they sat on the harbour wall with fish and chips. Ines said that her plan had left someone behind, and Jonah said that his was too slow.
Suddenly Ines had an idea, and she drew one fast main line on the paper bag. It had small, gentle branches that waited for people, and Jonah said, with shining eyes, that she had found the answer.
They went back to the office and worked through the night on a new joint plan. They called it fast spine, gentle branches, and by dawn it was the best plan either of them had ever made.
On Monday, Ines heard Jonah speaking quietly into his phone near the window. She caught the name Garrity and the words, Yes, I'll think about it, and her heart turned cold.
Ines marched across the office and said, in a shaking voice, that he had been using her all along. Jonah said he had turned the offer down, but she was too angry to listen.
Ines left the building without her coat and walked to the quay. She sat on a cold bench and watched the gulls, and she felt very small and very alone.
A voice beside her said hello, and it was old Alfie in his blue cap. He told her that Jonah had said no to Garrity, and that he had done it because of her.
Ines hurried back to the office, but Jonah's desk was empty. On her own desk lay the joint plan with a name on the cover that made her stop: Marlow and Pike.
The Board was meeting at the Harbour Hall in twenty minutes, and the rain was falling hard. Ines grabbed the plan and ran through the wet streets as fast as she could.
She burst into the hall, soaking wet, and walked straight to Jonah's side. Together they presented their plan, taking turns to speak, and they finished each other's sentences like old friends.
When they finished, the room was silent for a moment, and then the Board began to clap. They said that this plan was far better than Mr Garrity's cheap idea, and he left looking sour.
Mrs Faro stood up and said that she had wanted both of them all along. The Board had agreed to create two jobs, and the new Heads of Planning for Line 12 were Ines Marlow and Jonah Pike.

That evening they rode the first test tram on Line 12, with Alfie sitting happily in the front seat. In the golden light, Ines said she was sorry, and Jonah said it did not matter, and then they kissed.
Six months later, the first Line 12 tram ran on time and waited for everyone who ran. Back at the office, desks three and four now stood together, with Jonah's blue mug beside Ines's new yellow one.
C1C2: Ines Marlow always reached the Harbourgate Tram Company before anyone else, and she liked to stand at her window while the harbour slowly woke beneath her. For six years she had sat at desk three, planning the city's trams with a care that few of her colleagues had ever noticed. She believed, perhaps a little proudly, that a good timetable was a kind of promise kept.

On Monday morning the director, Mrs Faro, appeared in the doorway with a tall, easy-looking stranger at her side and led him to the empty desk that faced Ines's own. His name was Jonah Pike, and he had come from a smaller town to join the planners. Ines gave him a polite nod, but something inside her had already tightened like a drawn curtain.

Jonah hummed while he unpacked his things, a low and tuneless sound that drifted across the desks like warm air, and he sipped tea from a blue mug with a chip in its rim. Ines, who valued silence the way other people value money, found that she could not concentrate on a single column of numbers. It was ridiculous to be so annoyed by a stranger's good mood, and that made her even more annoyed.

At noon, Mrs Faro gathered the planners and announced that the city was at last building a new tram line, to be called Line 12. Whoever produced the best plan within eight weeks would become its Head of Planning, she said, and the Board would make the final choice. Every head turned, but Ines noticed that two of them turned toward each other, and that one of them was smiling.

Over sandwiches on the harbour wall, Ines declared to her friend Priya that the new job would be hers, however many evenings it cost her. Priya, who had known her long enough to see through such speeches, remarked gently that Ines already worked as though the building were on fire. A little rest, she suggested with a rueful smile, had never yet cost anyone a promotion, and might even help Ines win one.

For weeks the office printer had coughed and jammed, and Ines had written three polite emails about it without result. Jonah, within a minute of noticing the trouble, knelt beside it with a tiny screwdriver and coaxed it back to life, while the entire floor applauded. Ines clapped too, because it would have been rude not to, but the sound she made was thinner than she had intended.

Evening after evening, Ines remained at her desk long after the others had gone, drawing maps and checking figures by the glow of her lamp. Jonah, by contrast, packed his bag at exactly five and wandered off along the harbour as if the competition were a pleasant rumour. She watched him leave and wondered whether he was dangerously confident or simply a fool.

On Thursday, Ines hurried out to Gull Street at dawn to time how long pedestrians took to cross it, hoping to be the first planner to think of it. To her dismay Jonah was already standing on the corner with a clipboard, and in turning to look at him she walked straight into his arm. Their papers slipped from their hands and fluttered across the wet pavement like startled birds, while a passing cyclist rang his bell in protest.

Back in the office they argued over a map of the new line, Ines insisting that speed was everything and that fewer stops would carry more people to work. Jonah replied, in the same infuriatingly mild voice, that a city which ran too fast left its slowest citizens standing at empty stops. Neither of them raised a voice, yet the air between desks three and four had turned sharp.

The following week Mrs Faro invited each planner to describe an opening idea in ten minutes, and she listened with her chin resting on her hand. When they had finished, she praised both with generous warmth, yet she gave no hint whatever of a favourite. Ines left the room feeling as though she had run a race and been told only that the weather was fine.

One evening, when the office was empty, Ines allowed herself to open the shared folder and read through Jonah's draft. It was careful, imaginative and annoyingly kind, full of small touches she would never have thought of, and she closed it with a sinking, uncomfortable feeling. It is remarkably hard to hate a rival whose work you secretly admire, and harder still when he sits only two metres away.

The next morning Ines found a yellow note stuck to her map, with a small red circle drawn around a single street. Jonah had found an error in her measurements, a tiny slip of two metres that would have grown into a large problem later, and he had pointed it out without a word of mockery. She wanted very much to be angry about it, but the mistake was entirely her own, and the correction was exactly right.

Ines took a quiet revenge by lowering Jonah's chair to its lowest setting, so that he sank beside his desk like a man in a boat. The next morning her sad little desk plant had been carried to the sunniest windowsill, where it had already perked up and was stretching toward the light. It was impossible to tell who had won, and the whole office was watching.

On a grey Tuesday, torrents of rain flooded the tracks at Gull Street, and the whole line shuddered to a halt. Mrs Faro, with the air of someone who enjoyed her own cleverness, sent both planners out to improvise a temporary schedule and told them to share one umbrella. They squeezed into the first working tram, damp and silent, and found two seats facing each other.

As the rain drummed against the windows, Jonah admitted, almost shyly, that his grandfather had driven the old Line 9 for forty years. He held out his phone to show an old photograph of a beaming man in a navy uniform, one hand resting on his tram as if it were a favourite horse. For the first time, Ines saw that the cheerful rival across her desk had a reason for caring.

To her own surprise, Ines found herself telling him that she had grown up in a tiny flat above a laundry, where the windows steamed up all winter. As a girl she had counted the buses that passed below and dreamed of a city where every one of them arrived exactly when it had promised. She had never told anyone at work that story, and she was not sure why she was telling it now.

On Tuesday afternoon the ancient timetable software that everyone called the Clock froze, shuddered and went dark without a word of warning. Ines and Jonah, who had each been working in it all day, lost every number they had entered, and they stared at their blank screens in a rare moment of perfect agreement. Even the printer, which had survived so many crises, seemed to hold its breath while the office waited for the worst news to arrive.

With the deadline looming, they spread huge sheets of paper across the floor and rebuilt their timetables by hand, kneeling side by side with pencils behind their ears. Around midnight Jonah produced a slightly flattened sandwich from his bag, broke it in half without comment and passed one piece to Ines. She accepted it, and neither of them mentioned that they were, for once, working on the same side.

While they worked, they both noticed that the gradient of Quay Hill would slow any heavy tram to a crawl and spoil whichever timetable they built. They pointed at the same spot on the map at the very same moment, and their fingers touched, and both of them burst out laughing. It was the first time in weeks that Ines had laughed in that office.

Mrs Faro paused in the doorway and watched the pair of them laughing over a map, with an expression that was hard to read. She reminded them, kindly enough, that only one could become Head of Planning, and that she hoped friendship would not blur the contest. Then she wished them goodnight and left, and the laughter did not quite come back.

That night, in her small flat, Ines asked herself why winning mattered so much and found an answer she had not looked at for years. Her mother had scrubbed other people's offices after dark, and the young Ines had silently promised that one day she would sit at a desk of her own and be respected for it. The promotion, she realised, was less a prize than a debt of love she was still trying to repay.

The old Line 9 was due to close forever on Friday, and Jonah asked, a little awkwardly, whether she would ride it with him at sunrise. Ines refused at once, explaining that she had far too much work to waste a morning on nostalgia, and then she lay awake half the night regretting the answer. The truth was that she wanted to say yes more than she had wanted anything for weeks.

At five the next morning Ines gave up pretending to sleep, wrapped herself in a coat and walked through the cold streets to the Line 9 stop. Jonah was already waiting on the platform in a woollen scarf, holding two paper cups of tea, and he smiled as though he had never doubted that she would come. She took a cup, and neither of them said a word about the work.

On board they found an elderly man in a faded blue cap, upright in the front seat, and Jonah introduced him as his grandfather, Alfie. The old driver had come to say goodbye to the line that had filled forty years of his life, and he greeted Ines as if she were already part of the family. The tram creaked along its familiar route as the sky behind the harbour turned pink.

Alfie told stories all the way down the line, about runaway dogs, wedding parties and a passenger who had once tried to bring a goat aboard. Then his voice grew serious, and he said that the secret of a good tram was to wait a single moment for the person running toward it. A city, he said, is only as kind as its slowest minute, and a tram is the place where everyone can see it.

Ines crossed the little gap between their desks, swallowed her pride and asked whether she might use his idea of a waiting minute. Jonah looked startled, and then pleased, and then he told her to take it, since a good idea only does good when it is used. It was the most generous sentence anyone had said to her in months, and it left her strangely and thoroughly disarmed.

They agreed, there and then, to compete honestly, without tricks, secrets or hidden sabotage, and they sealed the bargain with a handshake. It lasted a few seconds longer than any handshake needed to last, and when they finally let go, Ines found that her hand felt oddly warm. Jonah studied the ceiling with intense interest, as though it contained something fascinating that he had somehow never noticed before.

With the Board presentation only two weeks away, the planners' floor hummed with late nights, cold coffee and the smell of takeaway food. Ines and Jonah sat opposite each other until long after dark, eating noodles from paper boxes and arguing cheerfully over every decimal point. It was the busiest and, though she would never have said so, the happiest she had been in years.

A ferocious storm swept in from the sea that night, rattling the windows and bending the lamp-posts along the harbour. Without warning the power failed, and the whole office dropped into darkness, leaving only Ines and Jonah and the roar of the wind. Jonah switched on the light of his phone and set it on the desk between them like a small, brave candle.

There is something about darkness that makes honesty easier, and they found themselves talking in low voices over the glowing phone. Jonah confessed that he had left his hometown for this chance and dreaded having nothing to show for it, while Ines admitted that her greatest fear was to remain ordinary, one more name on a long list of competent people. Each listened without trying to fix anything, which turned out to be exactly what the other needed.

They had drifted so close together that she could feel the warmth of his sleeve, and for one long moment neither of them moved or breathed. Then the lights flickered back on with a loud electric buzz, and both of them jumped away, suddenly fascinated by the maps on the walls. Neither of them spoke of it afterwards, but the silence that followed was somehow louder than the storm had ever been.

The following day, the two planners behaved like strangers, exchanging only the briefest of nods and keeping their eyes fixed on their screens. Priya, who missed very little, said nothing at all, but she placed a cup of strong tea on Ines's desk and squeezed her shoulder on the way past. It was the kindest sort of understanding, the kind that asks for nothing in return, and it very nearly undid Ines completely.

Mrs Faro summoned both planners to her office and, for once, did not smile. A consulting firm led by a Mr Garrity had offered the Board a cheap, ready-made plan, she explained, and unless the in-house planners truly impressed the members, the whole prize might slip out of the building. The room felt suddenly cold, and both of them sat up straighter, each privately wondering whether they had been fools to quarrel at all.

To settle the matter, Mrs Faro arranged a public trial on Saturday, when each plan would run for a morning on one stretch of the new line while the Board watched from a platform. Ines's fast timetable would take the first half of the day, and Jonah's careful one the second. Nothing anyone said, however clever, would carry as much weight as what the passengers actually did.

Saturday dawned bright and clear, and Ines's fast trams slid along the line with watch-like precision, every one of them exactly on time. Yet at the third stop a young woman pushing a pram arrived a moment too late, and the doors closed in front of her as the tram glided away. Ines saw the woman's disappointed face through the glass and felt her stomach drop, as if the tram had left without her own heart.

In the afternoon Jonah's gentle timetable took over, and his trams waited patiently at every stop until the last passenger had climbed aboard. Nobody was left behind, but the cars filled to bursting, and one weary driver complained to anyone who would listen that the whole line was falling behind. Jonah's smile faded as the minutes slipped by, and Ines, watching, could not enjoy it.

That evening they sat on the harbour wall with a paper bag of fish and chips between them, watching the boats nod in the dusk. Ines confessed that her plan had left a mother and baby on the platform, and Jonah admitted that his was too slow for the people who simply needed to get to work. It was strange, she thought, how much lighter the truth felt when it was shared.

Watching the lights come on across the water, Ines was struck by an idea, and she sketched it on the back of the paper bag. One fast main line would carry the crowds quickly, she explained, while a web of gentler branches would wait for the slow, the young and the tired. Jonah stared at the drawing, then at her, and said in a hushed voice that she had just solved the whole puzzle.

They returned to the office, switched on every lamp and worked through the night to turn the sketch into a real, workable plan. They named it fast spine, gentle branches, and as pale light crept over the harbour, they realised it was better than anything either of them could have built alone. Neither of them felt tired in the least, for the excitement of making something true carried them through the long hours.

On Monday morning Ines came back from the kitchen and heard Jonah speaking in a low voice into his phone beside the window. She caught the name Garrity and then the words, yes, I'll think about it, and everything in her turned cold and still. All her trust of the past weeks seemed to drain away in a single breath.

Ines strode across the floor and, in front of everyone, accused him of using her to build a plan he could sell to the other side. Jonah, white-faced, insisted that he had refused Garrity's offer, but the roaring in her ears was too loud, and she did not hear a word. The office fell so quiet that the printer's faint hum seemed to echo off the walls, and not one colleague dared to breathe.

She left the building without her coat and walked blindly to the quay, where the wind cut through her thin sleeves. On a cold wooden bench she watched the gulls wheel above the water, and the anger drained out of her, leaving only a hollow sense that she had done something unforgivable. She no longer knew whom she had been protecting, or from what, and she wished with all her heart that she could take back every word.

A familiar voice greeted her, and she looked up to find old Alfie settling beside her in his blue cap, a bag of crumbs for the gulls in his hand. He told her, in his mild way, that Jonah had refused Garrity's offer the very same day, because he would not betray a partner who had become a friend and something more. Ines covered her face with her hands, and for the first time that day she let herself cry, quietly and without shame.

Ines hurried back up the stairs, but Jonah's desk was empty, his blue mug sitting alone beside a darkened screen. On her own desk, however, lay a neatly bound copy of their joint plan, and on its cover were two names in careful letters: Marlow and Pike. A short note beneath it said, in his untidy handwriting, see you at the hall, whatever you decide, and I will understand either way.

The Board was due to meet at the Harbour Hall in twenty minutes, and the rain was pouring down in grey sheets. Ines snatched up the plan, ignored her umbrella and ran through the puddled streets, her heart pounding with a mixture of fear and hope. She had never in her life run so fast for anything that was not a tram.

She burst into the hall, soaked to the skin, and walked straight to the front, where Jonah stood alone with the plan in his hands. Without a word of apology yet spoken, she stood beside him, and together they presented their idea, trading sentences so naturally that the Board could hardly tell where one voice ended and the other began. Mr Garrity, sitting smugly in the third row, stopped smiling and began to look rather uncomfortable about his cheap ready-made plan.

When they finished, a long silence settled over the hall, and then, one by one, the Board members began to applaud. They declared that the plan was the best they had seen, far better than the consultant's cheap, ready-made proposal, and Mr Garrity gathered his papers and left with the expression of a man who had bitten a lemon. Behind the lectern, out of sight of the cheering Board, Ines felt Jonah's hand briefly find hers and hold it tightly.

Mrs Faro rose to her feet and confessed, with a twinkle, that she had known since the second week that Line 12 needed both of them. The Board had agreed to create two posts, she announced, and the new Heads of Planning would be Ines Marlow and Jonah Pike. Ines laughed and cried at the same moment, which is a very difficult thing to do in public.

That evening the first test tram slid along the shining new rails of Line 12, with Alfie in the front seat like an honoured guest. In the golden light that poured over the harbour, Ines whispered that she was sorry for everything, and Jonah answered that all he wanted was for her to sit beside him. When their lips finally met, the whole tram seemed to sigh with contentment, and Alfie, in the front seat, pretended with great dignity not to look.

Six months later the first public Line 12 tram rolled out of the depot exactly on time, and it paused, as promised, for a girl running with her school bag. Back at the office, desks three and four had been pushed together beneath the big window, where Jonah's chipped blue mug now sat beside Ines's cheerful new yellow one. The rival at desk four had become the person she most wanted to see each morning.
